# Known Issues

Repo-wide and cross-cutting issues only. Layer-specific gotchas live in dedicated
per-layer files (load only the one for your area):
- Compiler → `.github/memory/known-issues/compiler.md`
- IDE → `.github/memory/known-issues/ide.md`
- Razor → `.github/memory/known-issues/razor.md`

## Blank lines with whitespace fail linting

**Affected area:** all `*.cs` / `*.vb`
**Description:** Blank lines containing any space or tab fail lint/format; trailing whitespace also fails.
**Workaround:** Keep blank lines completely empty; run `dotnet format whitespace --folder . --include <path>`.

## Generated code must not be hand-edited

**Affected area:** `Syntax.xml`/`BoundNodes.xml`-derived `.cs`, `eng/common`, `*.xlf`
**Description:** These are produced by generators or external sync (DARC/Arcade); manual edits are overwritten or break builds.
**Workaround:** Edit the source (XML/`.resx`), then regenerate (`dotnet run --file eng/generate-compiler-code.cs`, or `/t:UpdateXlf` for `.xlf`). Never edit `eng/common` by hand.

## BuildValidator cannot replay post-compilation assembly weaving

**Affected area:** assemblies modified after `CoreCompile`
**Description:** BuildValidator reconstructs an assembly from its embedded compilation metadata. It cannot reproduce IL changes made afterward by tools such as BenchmarkDotNet's assembly weaver.
**Workaround:** Add narrowly scoped assembly exclusions to `eng/test-rebuild.ps1`; do not disable required post-compilation processing merely to make rebuild validation pass.

## IdeCoreBenchmarks requires BenchmarkDotNet 0.15 and .NET 10

**Affected area:** `src/Tools/IdeCoreBenchmarks`
**Description:** `Microsoft.VisualStudio.DiagnosticsHub.BenchmarkDotNetDiagnosers` implements the BenchmarkDotNet 0.15 exporter contract and fails to load with BenchmarkDotNet 0.16. BenchmarkDotNet 0.15 does not recognize a .NET 11 host, so the net10 benchmark executable must not use Roslyn's normal major-version roll-forward policy. BenchmarkDotNet's autogenerated runner only has a project reference to the benchmark host; central transitive pinning would otherwise replace the inherited 0.15 dependency with Roslyn's central 0.16 version.
**Workaround:** Keep the local BenchmarkDotNet 0.15 package overrides and `LatestPatch` runtimeconfig generation in `IdeCoreBenchmarks.csproj`. Benchmark validation must also override CI's ambient `DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=LatestMajor` for this project because environment variables take precedence over runtimeconfig settings. The project copies `BenchmarkDotNet.Directory.Packages.props` to its output as `Directory.Packages.props`; keep that local policy so generated runners use the same BenchmarkDotNet version as their host.

## TODO / PROTOTYPE comments are CI-gated

**Affected area:** whole repo, PRs targeting `main`
**Description:** CI flags `TODO` comments; PROTOTYPE comments are disallowed in PRs to `main`.
**Guidance:** Do **not** add new `TODO` or `TODO2` comments. Track follow-up work as a GitHub issue and link it in code (e.g. `// See https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/NNNN`). Existing `TODO2` markers are only a frozen baseline from when enforcement was introduced — they are not a pattern to copy. Remove all `PROTOTYPE` markers before merging to `main` (allowed only on feature branches).

## `artifacts/` DLLs can be locked by lingering build servers, MSBuild node-reuse workers, or orphaned BuildHost processes

**Affected area:** `folly.sh cleanse` / `folly.ps1 cleanse`
**Description:** Three independent mechanisms can leave a process holding `artifacts/` DLLs open across `folly` invocations, and they need three different fixes:
1. VBCSCompiler, the MSBuild build server, and the Razor build server register themselves as build servers and can hold an out-of-process BuildHost alive with `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild.Contracts.dll` / `...MSBuild.BuildHost.dll` loaded from `artifacts/`.
2. MSBuild node-reuse (`/nodeReuse`, default `true` when running locally, per `eng/common/tools.sh`/`.ps1`) leaves worker processes running after a build so the next one can reuse them. These are a completely separate mechanism from (1) — they never register as build servers, so nothing about build-server shutdown can see or stop them. Every `folly.sh`/`folly.ps1` build action passes `--nodeReuse false`/`-nodeReuse:$false` so folly's own builds clean up after themselves, but anything that builds/tests this repo outside `folly` (a bare `dotnet build`/`dotnet test`, an IDE background build, `dotnet run --file eng/generate-compiler-code.cs`) inherits the local default and leaves worker nodes resident.
3. `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild`'s `BuildHostProcessManager` (used by MSBuildWorkspace consumers, notably the LanguageServer's ProcessHost tests) launches its own on-demand `BuildHost` process as a plain `dotnet <path-to-Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild.BuildHost.dll>` child — shown as ".NET Host" in Windows Task Manager, with no obviously-attributable name. It's a third, separate mechanism from (1) and (2): it never registers as a build server (so `build-server shutdown` can't see it) and its own assembly is `MSBuild.BuildHost.dll`, not `MSBuild.dll` (so the node-reuse pattern in (2) doesn't match it either). If the process that spawned it (a test run, a debugger session) is killed or crashes without giving it a chance to exit, it survives indefinitely holding open the DLLs under its own `artifacts/bin/.../BuildHost-netcore/` output directory — the concrete symptom is `cleanse` reporting that specific `BuildHost-netcore` DLLs "could not be removed" with no other indication why.

On Windows an open handle blocks deleting the DLL outright; on Unix the file is simply unlinked out from under the process, so this is invisible there.

**Git-Bash/MSYS2 caveat:** most of `folly.sh`'s PID-finding for cleanse depends on `_cleanse_ps_snapshot` (and, for the ancestor-protection walk, `_cleanse_get_ppid`; and, for killing a matched PID's own children, `_cleanse_get_children`, used by `_cleanse_kill_pid_tree` for (1)-(3)'s survivors) returning full command lines / parent-child PID pairs. Plain `ps -eo pid,command`/`ps -o ppid= -p`/`ps -eo pid,ppid` is procps (GNU/Linux) and BSD (macOS) syntax; MSYS2/Cygwin's own `ps` has no `-o`/`-eo` custom-field support at all, and even with it, its default listing only reaches processes tracked through the MSYS/Cygwin runtime's own pid table — a BuildHost `dotnet <dll>` child spawned via .NET's own `Process.Start` (mechanism (3) above), or any native Windows child of a matched build-server/node-worker/BuildHost PID, never loads `msys-2.0.dll` and so was never in that table, meaning `cleanse` on Git-Bash could report success while a ".NET Host" (or an unreaped child of one) it had no way to see kept the DLLs open. `_cleanse_ps_snapshot`/`_cleanse_get_ppid`/`_cleanse_get_children` all detect this host (`is_windows_host`) and shell out to `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` via `pwsh`/`powershell.exe`/`powershell` on PATH instead — the same mechanism `folly.ps1` already uses — falling back to MSYS `ps -W` (parsed by its actual fixed columns, not `-eo`/`-o`; command-line arguments aren't available through `-W` either, so only the plain-name build-server pattern still matches through this fallback, not the DLL-substring BuildHost/node-reuse checks) only if no PowerShell is found at all. `-W`'s `PPID` (column 2) is Cygwin's own internal pid namespace, not the native Win32 one `WINPID` (column 4) and every pid this Windows-host code path otherwise passes around are in — `_cleanse_get_ppid`/`_cleanse_get_children`'s `-W` fallbacks build a Cygwin-pid → `WINPID` map from the whole snapshot and translate through it before returning anything, never handing column 2 back directly (see the bullet below for why an earlier pass got this wrong twice). `_cleanse_kill_tree` (Ctrl+C cleanup of cleanse's own scan/delete background jobs, a *different* helper from `_cleanse_kill_pid_tree`) is the deliberate exception and keeps plain `ps -eo pid,ppid | awk` unconditionally, even on a Windows host — see the "Kill mechanism" bullet below for why. Don't revert `_cleanse_ps_snapshot`/`_cleanse_get_ppid`/`_cleanse_get_children` to bare `ps -eo`/`ps -o ppid=` on the Windows-host branch, and don't route `_cleanse_kill_tree` onto the CIM path either — each is deliberate, in opposite directions, for a documented reason.

Getting PID discovery onto CIM wasn't sufficient by itself — two Codex review rounds on PR #87 caught seven more Windows-only bugs across the fix, all now addressed:
- **Path form mismatch:** `Win32_Process.CommandLine` is always a native path (`C:\repo\.dotnet\...`), never the MSYS-style path (`/c/repo/.dotnet/...`) `$scriptroot`/`$artifacts_dir` are on this host — a plain-text substring scope check against the MSYS form never matched the native one, so the CIM branch could enumerate a real match and then still fail to scope it, finding nothing. `cleanse` now computes `scriptroot_dotnet_scope`/`artifacts_scope` once via `cygpath -w` (falling back to the original MSYS-form strings if `cygpath` is unavailable) and scopes against those instead. NTFS paths are also case-insensitive at the OS level (unlike two Unix checkouts, which can legitimately differ only by casing), so `_cleanse_pids_matching_all`/`_cleanse_pids_matching_regex_and_substring` compare case-insensitively (`grep -Fi`) on a Windows host, matching `folly.ps1`'s own `$onWindows`-gated comparison.
- **Ancestor-walk seed:** the self-protection walk started from bash's own `$$`, which is MSYS/Cygwin's emulated pid and isn't guaranteed to be the native Win32 pid a CIM `ProcessId` filter expects — feeding it in directly could make the walk miss this script's real ancestors (its invoking shell, a CI wrapper) entirely, the exact process the exclusion exists to protect. A first fix tried resolving the real pid by spawning a PowerShell child and reading *its own* `ParentProcessId` via CIM inside a `$(...)` command substitution — but `$(...)` always forks a subshell to run whatever it wraps, so that "parent" was the transient substitution subshell, not this script's own persistent process, one hop short of where the walk needs to start (and possibly already exited by the time anything queried it). The actual fix needs no PowerShell at all: `native_self_pid` is read once, directly in the main shell via `read -r native_self_pid < /proc/self/winpid` (no `$(...)`, so no extra subshell) — MSYS/Cygwin's `/proc` exposes each process's real native pid at `/proc/<pid>/winpid` directly.
- **Kill mechanism:** `_cleanse_kill_pid_tree` signaled matched pids with bash's `kill -0`/`kill -TERM`/`kill -KILL`, which — like unpatched `ps` — only resolves pids in MSYS/Cygwin's own table; a CIM-discovered native pid (a BuildHost, or now a scoped-and-found build-server/node-worker) was invisible to it, so cleanse could find a survivor and then still fail to actually kill it. On a Windows host it now uses `tasklist`/`taskkill` (`_cleanse_native_alive`/`_cleanse_native_term`/`_cleanse_native_kill`) instead, which operate on real Win32 pids directly. `_cleanse_kill_tree` (the *separate* helper that only cleans up cleanse's own Ctrl+C-interrupted scan/delete background jobs, not (1)-(3)'s survivors) deliberately was **not** switched to this native/CIM path: `scan_pid`/`rm_pid` and their descendants are this bash process's own job-control children (`$!`), always MSYS-tracked pids regardless of host — routing that helper's child lookup through `_cleanse_get_children` (as an earlier commit briefly did) fed an MSYS pid into a CIM query keyed on native pids, a namespace mismatch that would silently find nothing; it's back to plain `ps -eo pid,ppid | awk` on purpose.
- **Self-matcher exclusion:** the Unix `ps` path always filtered out its own transient `grep` rows (`_cleanse_pids_matching_regex "$build_server_pattern"` runs as `_cleanse_ps_snapshot | grep -Ei ...`, and without the filter that `grep` process's own command line, containing the very pattern text, would match itself) — the first CIM branch didn't apply the same filter, so a build-server pattern search on Windows could count its own matcher process as a "build server," e.g. reporting one "stopped" via `dotnet build-server shutdown` when none was ever running. `_cleanse_exclude_self_matchers` (matching a bare or path-prefixed `grep`/`grep.exe`, since CIM's `CommandLine` is a full path unlike Unix `ps`'s bare `COMMAND` field) is now applied to every `_cleanse_ps_snapshot` branch, not just the plain-`ps` one. That filter's own regex needed a third round: it didn't match a *quoted* path (`"C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\grep.exe" ...`, exactly how CIM reports an executable under a space-containing directory like Git for Windows' default install), since the unquoted alternative can't itself contain spaces — nothing would mark where the path ends and arguments begin. The regex now has a dedicated quoted-path alternative alongside the unquoted one.
- **`_cleanse_get_children`'s no-PowerShell fallback and CRLF:** the initial CIM fix left this function's own no-PowerShell fallback on the same unsupported `ps -eo pid,ppid` syntax `_cleanse_ps_snapshot`'s fallback was fixed to avoid — corrected the same way, parsing `ps -W`'s fixed columns. Separately, its CIM branch returns multiple pids as separate lines, and Windows PowerShell (not pwsh 7+) writes those with CRLF endings — piping strips the trailing LF but leaves a stray `\r` on each pid, which then fails every `tasklist`/`taskkill` match against it by exactly one invisible character, silently leaving that child unsignaled. Fixed with `tr -d '\r'` (not `_cleanse_get_ppid`'s `tr -d '[:space:]'`, which would also delete the newlines separating multiple children into one unusable blob). `_cleanse_get_ppid` itself had the identical no-PowerShell gap (`ps -o ppid= -p` unconditionally, same unsupported syntax) missed in that same pass — fixed the same way.
- **`-W`'s `PPID`/`WINPID` are two different pid namespaces:** the first `ps -W` fallbacks for `_cleanse_get_ppid` and `_cleanse_get_children` above both compared/returned `PPID` (column 2) directly against a native pid — but column 2 is `-W`'s own Cygwin-internal pid, not the native Win32 one every other value in this Windows-host path is (`WINPID`, column 4; the pid arguments these functions are even called with). `_cleanse_get_ppid`'s fallback matched a native pid against `WINPID` correctly but then returned the matching row's raw `PPID` -- handing the *next* ancestor-walk iteration a Cygwin pid it would then compare against `WINPID` again, a mismatch that silently stops the walk one level too early. `_cleanse_get_children`'s fallback compared `PPID` directly against the native pid argument, the same cross-namespace comparison, silently finding no children at all. Both now build a Cygwin-pid → `WINPID` map from the entire `ps -W` snapshot in one pass and translate every value through it before returning, so nothing crosses back into the Cygwin namespace once it's left it.
- **Test harness PID translation:** `scripts/test-folly-cleanse.sh`'s own `_verify_pid_marker` (added to fix the coverage gap above) queried CIM/`ps -W` with `$!`-derived pids directly — but on Git-Bash, `$!` is an MSYS pid just like `folly.sh`'s own `$$`, not necessarily the native Win32 pid those native lookups key off of, so the verification could silently target the wrong process (or none) even after the coverage fix. Translated the same way `folly.sh` translates its own pid (`native_self_pid`): read `/proc/<pid>/winpid` before using it in either native lookup.
- **Termination-count accuracy on Windows:** `_cleanse_kill_pid_tree`'s Windows branch originally counted a pid as force-killed whenever it was alive at the start and gone by the end, without checking whether `_cleanse_native_term`/`_cleanse_native_kill` (`taskkill`) actually reported hitting it — if the target exited on its own in the window between the initial liveness check and the `taskkill` call (e.g. the shutdown RPC noted in mechanism (1) above took effect a little late), it would still get counted as "force-killed" despite cleanse never having signaled it, contradicting this function's own stated invariant (see the Unix branch's docstring). Now tracked via `taskkill`'s own exit code (`signaled`) and required alongside the final liveness check.
**Workaround:** `cleanse` runs `dotnet build-server shutdown` (resolving the repo-local `.dotnet/dotnet[.exe]` first, falling back to a global `dotnet` on `PATH`) for (1), then separately pattern-matches and kills any process whose command line references both this repo's own `.dotnet` SDK root and `MSBuild.dll` for (2), then a third pass matches any process whose command line references both this repo's own `artifacts/` directory and `MSBuild.BuildHost.dll` for (3) — cleanse never launches a build, test run, or BuildHost itself, so any such match is unconditionally stale. The (1) step reports what it did differently from (2) and (3): `build-server shutdown` always reports success whether or not anything was actually running, so its own output can't say what happened -- cleanse snapshots matching PIDs before and after the call and diffs them to report a real count. (2) and (3) instead enumerate workers/hosts once and kill each directly, counting only the ones `kill`/`Stop-Process` actually reports success on (not a before/after diff -- there's nothing else running that call could be racing). Either way, nothing is printed if there was nothing to report. Don't remove any of this when touching cleanse — without the shutdown/kill steps, deletion can intermittently fail on locked files with no other symptom.

`build-server shutdown` itself is not guaranteed to actually stop a server: it talks to the RPC pipe of servers registered by *the SDK it's invoked from*, so a build server started by a different dotnet install, or one whose RPC pipe is already wedged/orphaned, doesn't respond and survives the call silently while the CLI still reports success. Because of this, cleanse doesn't stop at diffing before/after PIDs to report a count for (1) — a PID gets force-killed directly (`Force-killed N build server process(es) that ignored 'dotnet build-server shutdown'.`) only once it satisfies all four: (a) it was already alive in the *original* pre-shutdown-call snapshot — a PID that only shows up in a later snapshot could be an unrelated process that started in between and must never be touched; (b) it's still alive after the shutdown call; (c) its command line references this checkout's own bootstrapped `.dotnet` SDK root, the same scope (2)'s node-reuse workers are held to — a build server for a *different* repo's checkout or SDK matches the VBCSCompiler/Razor name pattern just as easily but must never be killed, since cleanse has no way to know whether it's mid-compile for someone else's work (this scope check is case-sensitive on Unix and case-insensitive on Windows — `folly.ps1`'s `Get-PidsMatchingRegexAndSubstring` picks the comparison via `$onWindows`, matching `folly.sh`'s plain, case-sensitive `grep -F`, since two Unix checkouts can legitimately differ only by path casing); and (d) it isn't in this script's own ancestor process chain (`folly.sh`'s `_cleanse_ancestor_pids`, `folly.ps1`'s `Get-AncestorPids`, both walking the PPID chain from the running script's own PID up to *and including* PID 1) — an automation wrapper whose own command line happens to embed both the build-server name pattern and this checkout's `.dotnet` path (e.g. by echoing or defining them inline) would otherwise match its own invoking shell/CI agent and get force-killed, taking `cleanse` down with it. PID 1 is deliberately walked *into* the protected set, not just used as a loop-termination bound: in a container where the invoking CI agent is itself PID 1 (common for a container's entrypoint process), stopping the walk one step early would leave that PID unprotected, making it possible to kill the container's own init process out from under everything else running in it. Node-reuse worker candidates get the same (d) ancestor exclusion, even though they don't need (a)-(c)'s survivor logic, and the same case-sensitivity rule from (c) applies to `folly.ps1`'s `Get-PidsMatchingAll` (used for node-worker matching), not just `Get-PidsMatchingRegexAndSubstring` (used for build servers) — both were fixed together after review caught the first one and missed the second. Without the fallback at all, a build server left running by a foreign SDK or a stuck RPC pipe survives `cleanse` indefinitely with no error and no visible symptom beyond a `.NET host` process that never goes away; without the (a)-(d) scoping, the fallback itself becomes the hazard — collateral damage to an unrelated process, or worse, to the very shell running `cleanse`. The kill itself also isn't a fire-and-forget signal: both `folly.sh`'s `_cleanse_kill_pid_tree` and `folly.ps1`'s `Stop-ProcessTree` send a graceful stop first (`SIGTERM` / `Stop-Process` without `-Force`), wait up to 5 seconds, and only escalate to a forceful kill (`SIGKILL` / `Stop-Process -Force`) if the process is still alive — a count is only incremented once the PID is confirmed gone by re-checking AND this call actually had to signal it (a candidate that exited on its own between snapshot and kill attempt, e.g. because the shutdown RPC took effect a little late, was never force-killed by cleanse and must not be counted as if it were).

`folly.ps1`'s `Get-AncestorPids` builds its result as a `System.Collections.Generic.HashSet[int]` and must `return ,$result` (leading comma), never a bare `return $result`. PowerShell's pipeline output enumerates any `IEnumerable`, including a `HashSet` — a bare `return` on a collection with exactly one element silently unwraps it to a scalar (or `$null` if empty), so a caller's `$ancestorPids.Contains($_)` would throw under `ErrorActionPreference = Stop` the moment the ancestor chain happens to resolve to a single PID. The unary-comma wrapping is required *specifically* because the ancestor set can legitimately be small (a short-lived resolution failure breaks the PPID walk early) — a function returning the same collection type from a larger, more reliably multi-element source might not hit this in casual testing, which is exactly how it shipped unnoticed in the first place. Any future function here that returns a `HashSet`/array-like collection by reference (not via a `@()`-wrapped pipeline) needs the same guard.

`folly.sh` (bash) implements the PID search by shelling out to `ps | grep`, which needs two things to stay correct: (a) its own search `grep` process must be excluded from every snapshot, since the process being killed for having "VBCSCompiler" (or similar) in its command line is indistinguishable from the very `grep -Ei -- "VBCSCompiler|..."` process searching for it, which also carries that text in its own argv; (b) every `grep`/`comm` call whose match count can legitimately be zero (the common case) must be guarded (`|| true`) against `set -euo pipefail` treating "no match" as a fatal pipeline failure. Keep both when touching `folly.sh`'s cleanse.

`folly.ps1`'s process matching (`Get-ProcessSnapshot`) uses `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` on Windows and falls back to shelling out to `ps -eo pid,ppid,command` (the same source `folly.sh` uses) everywhere else. Before that fallback existed, `folly.ps1` called `Get-CimInstance` unconditionally — since that cmdlet is Windows-only WMI and PowerShell Core on Linux/macOS has no CIM server, it threw immediately and the *entire* cleanse action failed outright. This went unnoticed for a while because `folly.ps1` had never actually been run in a non-Windows sandbox; PRs touching it could only claim "written for parity, not runnable here". The `ps`-based fallback fixes that. It initially had no self-exclusion for the invoking shell: if whatever launched `pwsh` had the search text (e.g. "VBCSCompiler") anywhere in *its own* command line — not `folly.ps1`'s own invocation, but an ancestor shell's — that ancestor would match and get force-killed too. This isn't a concern for a normal terminal/CI invocation, but showed up hard when testing cleanse from Claude Code's own sandbox, where the harness wraps every Bash tool call as a single `bash -c '<entire command text>'`, so a test script that so much as defines the pattern string inline (e.g. in a heredoc) embeds it into that wrapper's own argv and makes the wrapper itself a match — which is exactly what led to adding the `Get-AncestorPids`/`_cleanse_ancestor_pids` exclusion described above, rather than leaving this as a testing-only gotcha. When testing cleanse's build-server/node-worker killing logic in an agent sandbox, still prefer launching the fake target process from a separate script file (`exec -a ... /path/to/script.sh`) rather than inline in the same tool call that contains the search pattern text — the ancestor exclusion protects the *invoking* shell chain, not a sibling test-runner process whose own argv happens to match.

## `folly.sh cleanse`'s live progress must never share a pipe with the deletion it's reporting on

**Affected area:** `folly.sh cleanse`'s GNU-`find` branch (`_cleanse_read_rm_log` and its background `find -delete` job).

**Description:** an earlier version had `find -depth -type f -printf '%s\n' -delete` write each deleted file's size to a named pipe (`mkfifo`), with this shell's own `while read` loop consuming it and periodically calling `format_bytes` (an `awk` spawn) to redraw the progress line. A pipe has a small, fixed kernel buffer (64 KiB on Linux — a few thousand short lines). `find` was writing to that pipe as fast as the filesystem allowed, but every time the reader paused to spawn `awk` for a redraw, the reader fell behind, the pipe filled, and `find`'s *next* `write()` call blocked until the reader drained it — because a full pipe blocks its writer. That's not merely a slow or jumpy display: it's the actual deletion visibly stopping and restarting in lockstep with the reader's own pace, reported as "it deletes files, then stops, then starts, then stops" (nothing to do with how often the line redraws — even a single, well-paced redraw per second was enough to trigger it once `find` was fast enough to fill the pipe in that gap).

**Workaround:** `find`'s background job now appends to a plain regular file instead of a named pipe (`> "$rm_log"`, no `mkfifo`). A regular file has no such backpressure — the kernel buffers writes to it and never blocks the writer on a slow or entirely absent reader — so `find` now runs completely unthrottled by the display. The display loop (only entered when `interactive`) independently polls that file on its own timer (`sleep 0.2`, matching the scan spinner above it, gated to redraw at most once per wall-clock `$SECONDS` tick) via `_cleanse_read_rm_log`, which sums the log's size column with a fresh `awk` pass each poll — cheap relative to `find`'s own work, and touching only the log file, never the filesystem `find` is racing against (unlike the old rescan-based BSD/non-GNU fallback this deliberately avoids repeating that mistake for — see the CONVENTIONS.md `cleanse` progress note). The two processes are fully decoupled, the way two ordinary background jobs would be, rather than forced into lockstep by a shared pipe. Don't reintroduce a pipe (`mkfifo`) between `find` and this shell for this purpose, even for a "simpler" single-process design — the backpressure is inherent to how pipes work, not a bug in how the old code used one.

**A trailing newline on `_cleanse_read_rm_log`'s `awk` output is required, not cosmetic:** bash's `read` returns non-zero when it hits EOF before a newline, even though it still populates the target variables from whatever partial data it read — so `awk '{...} END{printf "%d %d", s+0, n+0}'` (no `\n`) makes every `read -r deleted_bytes deleted_count < <(_cleanse_read_rm_log)` call fail, which aborts the whole script under `set -e`/`pipefail` the moment it's reached. This was caught by `scripts/test-folly-cleanse.sh` immediately (5 of 9 cases failing with no output at all) — a strong signal that any future process-substitution `read` added to `cleanse` needs a matching trailing-newline check on its producer's output format before it's considered done.

## `eng/build.ps1`'s `-testInteractiveConsole` has no `eng/build.sh` counterpart, and that's correct

**Affected area:** `eng/build.sh` vs `eng/build.ps1`, `folly.sh scry` vs `folly.ps1 scry`
**Description:** `eng/build.ps1` has a `-testInteractiveConsole` switch with no `eng/build.sh` counterpart. This looks like `folly.sh`/`folly.ps1` parity drift, but it isn't — it exists to solve a problem that only occurs in PowerShell's execution model: it works around `Exec-CommandCore`'s default behavior of redirecting `RunTests`' stdout and relaying it line-by-line through `Write-Output`, which makes `RunTests` see `Console.IsOutputRedirected = true` and disables its live per-work-item progress table. `eng/build.sh` invokes `RunTests.dll` with a direct foreground `dotnet exec` and no capture/relay step, so `RunTests` already sees a real inherited console by default when run via `folly.sh scry` — there is nothing for an equivalent switch to opt out of.
**Guidance:** Do not "fix" this by porting the switch to `eng/build.sh` — it would be an inert no-op there. If `eng/build.ps1` ever changes how it uses it, re-verify this reasoning still holds rather than assuming the two scripts have simply drifted apart.

By contrast, `eng/build.sh` **does** now have all of: a Framework (`.NET Framework`/net472) test leg (`--testDesktop`, mirroring `-testDesktop`/`-testIOperation` fallback in `eng/build.ps1`), `$FOTU_TEST_RESULTS_SUFFIX` env var handling (giving each of `folly.sh scry`'s Core/Framework legs its own `TestResults`/log directory), and `--testSuppressConsoleSummary` (forwarded to `RunTests --suppressConsoleSummary`, see `Options.SuppressConsoleSummary`/`TestRunner.Print` in `src/Tools/RunTests/`). These were ported deliberately so `folly.sh scry` can run both legs on a Windows host running bash (e.g. Git Bash/MSYS2), not just via `folly.ps1`: `--testDesktop` still only works on a genuine Windows host (net472 has no cross-platform runtime) — both `eng/build.sh` and `folly.sh` reject it outright (`is_windows_host`/`$OSTYPE`+`uname -s` check) on any other host rather than attempting it and failing deep inside `RunTests` — and when both legs run, `folly.sh` passes `--testSuppressConsoleSummary` to suppress each leg's own live final PASSED/FAILED/TIMEOUT table (still written to its log file) so its own combined-summary block (reading both legs' tables back from their log files) is the only place either table prints, instead of each leg's table printing live and then getting duplicated by that combined block. When `folly.sh scry` runs only one leg, `both_legs` is false, `--testSuppressConsoleSummary` is never passed, and that leg's own live table prints normally with nothing to combine it with.

## Git-for-Windows' bash (MSYS2) mangles Arcade's `/`-prefixed MSBuild switches

**Affected area:** `folly.sh` on Windows, invoked from Git Bash rather than WSL
**Description:** `eng/common/tools.sh`'s `MSBuild` function (Arcade-vendored — never hand-edited, see the
generated-code entry above) invokes `MSBuild.exe` with classic single-slash switches:
`/m /nologo /clp:Summary /v:$verbosity /nr:$node_reuse ...`. Git-for-Windows' bash is built on MSYS2,
which auto-converts any `/`-prefixed argument into a Windows path before handing it to a native
(non-MSYS) executable, on the assumption it's a Unix path meant for something expecting a Windows one.
`MSBuild.exe` is exactly such a native executable, and its own switches are exactly what this heuristic
misfires on — `/nologo` has been observed mangled into `C:/Program Files/Git/nologo` (the MSYS
install root prepended, as if `/nologo` were a Unix path rooted there), producing errors like
`MSB1008: Only one project can be specified` from switches that arrived as extra positional
arguments instead of being parsed as switches at all. This is specific to real Git-Bash/MSYS2 — WSL's
bash is a genuine Linux userland with no such translation layer (unaffected), and native Linux/macOS
bash has no MSYS runtime at all (`$MSYSTEM` is simply unset there).
**Workaround:** `folly.sh` exports `MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*'` (disabling MSYS's path-conversion heuristic
entirely for the rest of the process) whenever `$MSYSTEM` is set, before ever invoking `eng/build.sh`.
Do not "fix" this in `eng/common/tools.sh` itself — it's Arcade-synced and any hand-edit is overwritten.
If a genuinely Windows-Unix-path argument ever needs to reach a native tool from `folly.sh` on Git Bash
after this env var is set, it will need an explicit `cygpath`/similar conversion at the call site instead
of relying on MSYS's automatic (and, for MSBuild specifically, actively harmful) behavior.

## Environmental test failures (not code bugs)

**Affected area:** full `test.sh`/`Test.cmd` runs
**Description:** A few tests fail for environment reasons unrelated to changes:
- `RuntimeHostInfoTests.DotNetInPath_Symlinked` requires symlink-creation privilege (run elevated).
- `Workspaces.MSBuild` `NewlyCreatedProjectsFromDotNetNew.Validate*TemplateProjects` fail without mobile (ios/tvos/macos/maccatalyst) dotnet workloads installed.
**Workaround:** Prefer targeted test projects; treat these specific failures as environmental.
